\chapter{Which One in the Line}
\label{ch:bn-ordinals}
\hlchaptermodality{38}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say first to fifth in Bengali, put an ordinal in front of a noun without changing it, and say which layer of the language every one of them comes from.}

Complete BN-R27-first-to-fifth, run prothom to ponchom, and say which one of the five you could have built from a number you already had.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ditiyô]{\bn{দ্বিতীয়} (ditiyô) — second, and the second layer it comes from}

\label{lesson:BN-C27-ditiyo}



\begin{quote}
A second kind of number word starts here, so the recalls come first, at the three growing distances this book can measure.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\bn{থ}} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{he, she} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{welcome} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{দ্বিতীয়}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{দ্বিতীয়}} — \emph{ditiyô} — \textbf{second}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{দ্বিতীয়} \bn{জামাটা}} — \emph{ditiyô jāmāṭā} — \textbf{the second shirt}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\bn{দুই}} answers \emph{how many}. \textbf{\bn{দ্বিতীয়}} answers \emph{which one in the line}, and it stands in front of its noun and never changes, the way \textbf{\bn{লাল}} does. No agreement to learn.

Read the spelling and the romanization again, because they disagree: written \textbf{\bn{দ্ব}}-, said \emph{di}-. The cluster is on the page and gone from the mouth.

\begin{cousinweb}
Chapter twelve told you two things about the old Sanskrit \emph{dv-}: that it is gone from the everyday numeral in Bengali, Hindi and Marathi alike, and that it is \textbf{alive in words borrowed straight back out of Sanskrit}. It gave you \textbf{\bn{দ্বার}} \emph{dvār}, \textquotedblleft{}door\textquotedblright{}, as its example and left it there.

\textbf{\bn{দ্বিতীয়}} is another of those words, and this time it is a number.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{layer} & \textbf{two} & \textbf{second} \\
\midrule
everyday, inherited & \textbf{\bn{দুই}} \emph{dui} & — \\
borrowed back from Sanskrit & — & \textbf{\bn{দ্বিতীয়}} \emph{ditiyô} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Bengali keeps \textbf{two layers of number word}. You count in the inherited one; every ordinal in this chapter comes out of the other. That is why none of the five will look much like the numbers you already say.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dui}, then \emph{ditiyô}
  \item \emph{ditiyô jāmāṭā}
  \item what is written and what is said — \emph{dva} on the page, \emph{di} in the mouth
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many layers of number word does Bengali keep? (\textbf{Two}.) Which one do you count in? (\textbf{The inherited one} — \emph{ek, dui, tin, chār, pā̃ch}.) Does \textbf{\bn{দ্বিতীয়}} change its ending for the noun? (\textbf{No} — like \textbf{\bn{লাল}}, it never changes.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A6\%A6\%E0\%A7\%8D\%E0\%A6\%AC\%E0\%A6\%BF\%E0\%A6\%A4\%E0\%A7\%80\%E0\%A7\%9F}{Wiktionary: \bn{দ্বিতীয়}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tritiyô]{\bn{তৃতীয়} (tritiyô) — third, and an ending that now has two members}

\label{lesson:BN-C27-tritiyo}



\begin{quote}
Four recalls, then the second half of a pair.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{second} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{here} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the respectful \emph{he, she} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{red} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{তৃতীয়}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{তৃতীয়}} — \emph{tritiyô} — \textbf{third}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{তৃতীয়} \bn{লাল} \bn{জামাটা}} — \emph{tritiyô lāl jāmāṭā} — \textbf{the third red shirt}
\end{quote}

Two adjectives now stand in front of one noun, and neither of them changes. Say \textbf{\bn{তিন}}, then \textbf{\bn{তৃতীয়}}: the \textbf{\bn{ত}} carries over and almost nothing else does.

Same disagreement between page and mouth as last lesson, in a smaller way: the \textbf{\bn{ৃ}} under the \textbf{\bn{ত}} is written and the \emph{r} it stands for is not said.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built: -\bn{তীয়} is a shape, not a coincidence}]
Set the two side by side and the tails match:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{ordinal} & \textbf{Sanskrit word it was borrowed from} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\bn{দ্বিতীয়}} — \emph{ditiyô} & \emph{dvitīya} \\
\textbf{\bn{তৃতীয়}} — \emph{tritiyô} & \emph{tṛtīya} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Wiktionary calls \textbf{\bn{তৃতীয়}} a learned borrowing from Sanskrit \emph{tṛtīya} in those words. Two Sanskrit words ended alike, in \emph{-tīya}, and the two Bengali words borrowed from them end alike too, in \textbf{-\bn{তীয়}}.

One word ending a certain way is a fact about that word. Two is a shape, and this is the second — which is why the ending is being named now and was not named last lesson.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tin}, then \emph{tritiyô}
  \item \emph{ditiyô}, \emph{tritiyô} — the pair, back to back
  \item \emph{tritiyô lāl jāmāṭā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is left of \textbf{\bn{তিন}} inside \textbf{\bn{তৃতীয়}}? (\textbf{The \bn{ত}}.) How many words share the \textbf{-\bn{তীয়}} ending so far? (\textbf{Two}.) Why was the ending not named one lesson earlier? (\textbf{One word is not a shape}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A6\%A4\%E0\%A7\%83\%E0\%A6\%A4\%E0\%A7\%80\%E0\%A7\%9F}{Wiktionary: \bn{তৃতীয়}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[choturthô]{\bn{চতুর্থ} (choturthô) — fourth, on an ending of its own}

\label{lesson:BN-C27-choturtho}



\begin{quote}
Four recalls, then an ordinal that will not join the pair.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{third}, and the ending it shares — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{there} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{him, her}, of the one standing there — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{blue} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{চতুর্থ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{চতুর্থ}} — \emph{choturthô} — \textbf{fourth}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{চতুর্থ} \bn{নীল} \bn{জামাটা}} — \emph{choturthô nīl jāmāṭā} — \textbf{the fourth blue shirt}
\end{quote}

Say \textbf{\bn{চার}}, then \textbf{\bn{চতুর্থ}}. Two pieces cross over this time, the \textbf{\bn{চ}} and the \textbf{\bn{র}}, which is more of its number than any ordinal you have met keeps. The tail is \textbf{\bn{থ}} — the letter this book waited longest for, and its second job in five lessons.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built: three endings, and only one of them repeats}]
Samsad's \emph{Bengali-English Dictionary} gives \textbf{\bn{চতুর্থ}} its own headword and romanizes it \emph{caturtha} — the Sanskrit word carried over with nothing altered. Same layer as the last two, different ending:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{ending} & \textbf{words} \\
\midrule
\textbf{-\bn{তীয়}} & \textbf{\bn{দ্বিতীয়}}, \textbf{\bn{তৃতীয়}} \\
\textbf{-\bn{র্থ}} & \textbf{\bn{চতুর্থ}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

One member, so this book will not call it a pattern. It is named so you can see that the borrowed layer arrived with \textbf{more than one shape in it} — Sanskrit did not build all its ordinals the same way, and Bengali took them as they were.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chār}, then \emph{choturthô}
  \item \emph{ditiyô}, \emph{tritiyô}, \emph{choturthô} — two tails, then a third
  \item \emph{choturthô nīl jāmāṭā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many endings have the four ordinals shown so far? (\textbf{Two} — \textbf{-\bn{তীয়}} twice and \textbf{-\bn{র্থ}} once.) Which layer are they all from? (\textbf{The borrowed Sanskrit one}.)

Sources: \href{https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/biswas-bengali\_query.py?qs=\%E0\%A6\%9A\%E0\%A6\%A4\%E0\%A7\%81\%E0\%A6\%B0\%E0\%A7\%8D\%E0\%A6\%A5\&searchhws=yes}{Samsad Bengali-English Dictionary, \bn{চতুর্থ}, p. 346 (DSAL)}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[prothom]{\bn{প্রথম} (prothom) — first, and an irregularity Bengali inherited whole}

\label{lesson:BN-C27-prothom}



\begin{quote}
Four recalls, then the word with nothing of its number in it.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{fourth} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} ask \emph{where?} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{his, her} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{black} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{প্রথম}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{প্রথম}} — \emph{prothom} — \textbf{first}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{প্রথম} \bn{কালো} \bn{জামাটা}} — \emph{prothom kālo jāmāṭā} — \textbf{the first black shirt}
\end{quote}

Say \textbf{\bn{এক}}, then \textbf{\bn{প্রথম}}. Not one sound crosses over. \textbf{\bn{তৃতীয়}} kept its \textbf{\bn{ত}}, \textbf{\bn{চতুর্থ}} kept a \textbf{\bn{চ}} and a \textbf{\bn{র}}, and this word keeps nothing.

It carries an everyday second use too: \emph{earliest, chief, best} — \emph{first in the class} as much as \emph{first in the line}.

\begin{cousinweb}
Wiktionary calls \textbf{\bn{প্রথম}} a learned borrowing from Sanskrit \emph{prathama}, in the same words it uses for \textbf{\bn{তৃতীয়}}. So all four ordinals so far come out of the same shelf, and three of them are built on their own Sanskrit number: \emph{dvitīya} on \emph{dvi}, \emph{tṛtīya} on \emph{tri}, \emph{caturtha} on \emph{catur}.

\emph{prathama} is not built on anything of the kind. Sanskrit's word for \textbf{one} was \emph{eka} — the word \textbf{\bn{এক}} still is — and \emph{prathama} has never shared a sound with it. The gap you are looking at is \textbf{older than Bengali}: Bengali borrowed the word entire, hole and all, and had no hand in making it.

Had this word come first you would have had to take it as a Bengali oddity. Coming fourth, after a shape has held twice and a second ending has appeared once, it can be read for what it is.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ek}, then \emph{prothom} — and notice nothing carries over
  \item \emph{prothom}, \emph{ditiyô}, \emph{tritiyô}, \emph{choturthô}
  \item \emph{prothom kālo jāmāṭā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How much of \textbf{\bn{এক}} is inside \textbf{\bn{প্রথম}}? (\textbf{None}.) Whose gap is it? (\textbf{Sanskrit's} — Bengali borrowed the word as it stood.) What else can \textbf{\bn{প্রথম}} mean? (\emph{Earliest, chief, best}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A6\%AA\%E0\%A7\%8D\%E0\%A6\%B0\%E0\%A6\%A5\%E0\%A6\%AE}{Wiktionary: \bn{প্রথম}}; \href{https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/biswas-bengali\_query.py?qs=\%E0\%A6\%AA\%E0\%A7\%8D\%E0\%A6\%B0\%E0\%A6\%A5\%E0\%A6\%AE\&searchhws=yes}{Samsad Bengali-English Dictionary, \bn{প্রথম}, p. 682 (DSAL)}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nyô]{\bn{ঞ} — the nasal of the \bn{চ} row}

\label{lesson:BN-W06-nya}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\bn{চ}}, \textbf{\bn{জ}} and \textbf{\bn{ন}}. Say where each one is made.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{first} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{white} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\bn{ঞ}
\end{quote}

Chapter thirty-seven drew a square: \textbf{\bn{ত} \bn{থ} \bn{দ} \bn{ধ}}, four letters made in one place, sorted by voice and breath. A row of the Bengali grid has a \textbf{fifth} member — a nasal made in that same place. For the teeth row it is \textbf{\bn{ন}}, and you have been writing it since the first word in this book.

\textbf{\bn{ঞ}} is the fifth member of a different row, the one whose letters are made with the tongue flat against the roof of the mouth:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the row} & \textbf{letters you have} \\
\midrule
voiceless & \textbf{\bn{চ}} \emph{chô}, \textbf{\bn{ছ}} \emph{chhô} \\
voiced & \textbf{\bn{জ}} \emph{jô} \\
\textbf{nasal} & \textbf{\bn{ঞ}} \emph{nyô} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say \textbf{\bn{চ}} and then hum through your nose without moving your tongue. That is \textbf{\bn{ঞ}}.

You will almost never meet it standing on its own. In modern Bengali it does its work joined to the letter beside it, and the joining you need is \textbf{\bn{ঞ্চ}} — \textbf{\bn{ঞ}} with \textbf{\bn{চ}}, the nasal in front of the stop it is made with. That is the next lesson's word.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{ঞ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\bn{চ}}, then \textbf{\bn{ঞ}} — same place, the nose opened
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{ঞ্চ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the three nasals this book now has — \textbf{\bn{ন}}, \textbf{\bn{ঞ}}, and the chandrabindu \textbf{\bn{ঁ}}, which is a nasal with no letter of its own
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where is \textbf{\bn{ঞ}} made? (\textbf{Where \bn{চ} is} — the tongue on the roof of the mouth.) What makes it different from \textbf{\bn{চ}}? (\textbf{The nose is open}.) Which joined form will you need? (\textbf{\bn{ঞ্চ}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ponchom]{\bn{পঞ্চম} (ponchom) — fifth, and the two layers touching}

\label{lesson:BN-C27-ponchom}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then the word the last lesson bought a letter for.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\bn{ঞ}}, and say where it is made — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{we} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{green} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{পঞ্চম}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{পঞ্চম}} — \emph{ponchom} — \textbf{fifth}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{পঞ্চম} \bn{সবুজ} \bn{জামাটা}} — \emph{ponchom sobuj jāmāṭā} — \textbf{the fifth green shirt}
\end{quote}

There is the \textbf{\bn{ঞ্চ}} you wrote last lesson, between a \textbf{\bn{প}} and a \textbf{\bn{ম}}. Its outline is one you already know: \textbf{\bn{প}} … nasal … \textbf{\bn{চ}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
Samsad's dictionary has the entry this chapter has been building towards. Its headword is \textbf{\bn{পঞ্চ}} \emph{ponchô}, glossed \textbf{five}, with \textbf{\bn{পঞ্চম}} listed under it as \textbf{fifth}. The borrowed layer has its own \emph{five}, and its \emph{fifth} is built on it. Put the two fives one above the other:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{layer} & \textbf{five} \\
\midrule
borrowed from Sanskrit & \textbf{\bn{পঞ্চ}} — \emph{ponchô} \\
everyday, inherited & \textbf{\bn{পাঁচ}} — \emph{pā̃ch} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Same \textbf{\bn{প}}. Same \textbf{\bn{চ}}. Between them, in the borrowed word a whole letter, \textbf{\bn{ঞ}}; in the everyday word the \textbf{\bn{ঁ}} you were told in chapter twelve was \textquotedblleft{}the chandrabindu, nasalising the vowel\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\bn{পাঁচ} is \bn{পঞ্চ} with the nasal letter worn down into a moon-dot}, and that is not a guess. Wiktionary's entry for \textbf{\bn{পাঁচ}} writes its Sanskrit source as \textbf{\bn{পঞ্চ}} and walks the road between them: \emph{pañca}, then \emph{paṃca}, then a Middle Bengali form already spelled with the mark, then \textbf{\bn{পাঁচ}}. The letter thins to a nasal sign and then to a nasal vowel.

The two layers this chapter opened with are not two vocabularies that happen to sit side by side. In this word you can watch one of them turning into the other, and the whole of the evidence is four letters wide.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{pā̃ch}, then \emph{ponchô}, then \emph{ponchom}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{পঞ্চম}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ponchom sobuj jāmāṭā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textbf{\bn{পঞ্চম}} built on? (\textbf{\bn{পঞ্চ}}, the borrowed \emph{five}.) And what is \textbf{\bn{পাঁচ}}? (\textbf{The same word}, worn down.) Which ordinal in this chapter is built on no number at all? (\textbf{\bn{প্রথম}}.)

Sources: \href{https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/biswas-bengali\_query.py?qs=\%E0\%A6\%AA\%E0\%A6\%9E\%E0\%A7\%8D\%E0\%A6\%9A\&searchhws=yes}{Samsad Bengali-English Dictionary, \bn{পঞ্চ}, p. 604 (DSAL)}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A6\%AA\%E0\%A6\%BE\%E0\%A6\%81\%E0\%A6\%9A}{Wiktionary: \bn{পাঁচ}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{First to fifth, in order at last}

\label{lesson:BN-R27-first-to-fifth}



\begin{quote}
Four recalls before the run.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{fifth} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{second}, and which layer it comes from — \textbf{R2}, six lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{you}, more than one — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\bn{লাল}} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}

Nothing new arrives here. This is the first time the five stand in numerical order, and that has been deliberate.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{prothom ditiyô tritiyô choturthô ponchom} — the run, without stopping
  \item the two endings — \textbf{-\bn{তীয়}} twice, \textbf{-\bn{র্থ}} once
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter, in one table}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the layer you count in} & \textbf{the layer the ordinals come from} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\bn{এক}} \emph{ek} & \textbf{\bn{প্রথম}} \emph{prothom} \\
\textbf{\bn{দুই}} \emph{dui} & \textbf{\bn{দ্বিতীয়}} \emph{ditiyô} \\
\textbf{\bn{তিন}} \emph{tin} & \textbf{\bn{তৃতীয়}} \emph{tritiyô} \\
\textbf{\bn{চার}} \emph{chār} & \textbf{\bn{চতুর্থ}} \emph{choturthô} \\
\textbf{\bn{পাঁচ}} \emph{pā̃ch} & \textbf{\bn{পঞ্চম}} \emph{ponchom} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read the last row again. Those two are the \textbf{same word} at two ends of a long road, and the difference between them is a letter you learned two lessons ago turning into a mark you learned in chapter twelve.

The chapter cost exactly one new letter, \textbf{\bn{ঞ}}, and spent it on the row that proves the point.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which layer are all five ordinals from? (\textbf{The borrowed Sanskrit one}.) Which of them has no number inside it at all? (\textbf{\bn{প্রথম}} — and the gap is Sanskrit's, not Bengali's.) Which two rows of the table are the same word? (\textbf{\bn{পাঁচ}} and \textbf{\bn{পঞ্চ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
